My viewpoint is that if settlers do not want to honour treaty, they are always more than welcome to depart from that treaty territory. 

These rights held by Indigenous peoples are a form of continued rent/mortgage on ceded lands and on treaty land.

These treaties were rarely negotiated in good faith, and Indigenous peoples were generally not expected to exist as distinct peoples long enough to greatly benefit from the rights, but unfortunately, we did not disappear, and we still hold those rights.

I particularly get annoyed at owners of fishing launch businesses & resorts back home in Minnesota, saying that Indigenous nations, if left unchecked, would overfish lakes to exhaustion.

These owners’ businesses are not built on *their* customers coming and not taking lots of fish out of the lake.

The settler who shouts about “special treatment” because he cannot fish over the limit or cannot fish on a lake or in an inlet is quick to forget that it is more likely than not that the body of water likely was in an extremely impaired state or would be if it weren’t for Indigenous monitoring.

There are far more overtly racist arguments, naturally. The idea that Indigenous peoples hold “special rights” that settlers do not have is another common statement in reference to Indigenous rights. Some have even referred to these rights as “apartheid”, a very poor use of the word, in my opinion.

The conservation angle has been a particularly effective way of mobilizing settlers against Indigenous environmentally based treaty rights, as they can easily deny any racial animosity, but rather couch their concerns as being focused on biodiversity and conservation.

Well, they’ve generally tried to constrain Indigenous rights in general, but fishing & hunting rights seem to be an area that particularly draws settler ire.

The refrain usually is “If you allow the Natives to take all of the _____, there won’t be any left for the rest of us!

From the fish-ins in Washington in the 1960s to the Walleye War in Wisconsin in the 1980s, to Mille Lacs v. Minnesota in the 90s, to confrontations between Indigenous fishermen and settler fisherman in Nova Scotia in 2021, the settler state has sought to constrain Indigenous rights related to fish.

A number of years ago when I was on Twitter, I had a tweet go
viral; it talked about the confrontations between Mik’maw and settler fishermen in the Maritimes.

Essentially, I poked fun at settler fears of overfishing by Indigenous peoples.

Let’s get something out of the way to begin—the above graphic is disingenuous and made in bad faith. The group that posted it, a “fishermen” organization from Sidney, just up the peninsula from me, is clearly using dog whistles to target Indigenous fishing and treaty rights. 

But why?

I saw this graphic on my Facebook feed, and I had to marvel at the sheer timing of it.
